GLOBAL.name: No country specified
notes: No jurisdiction-specific labelling rules applied. Specify a country for a sharper verdict.

AE.name: United Arab Emirates
notes: UAE.S GSO 2055-1 defines the national halal standard; the National Halal Mark is administered by MOIAT.
Imported food must be registered, and pork products are restricted to designated sections of licensed retailers.
Arabic labelling is mandatory, so ingredient names may appear only in Arabic.

SA.name: Saudi Arabia
notes: SFDA enforces GSO halal requirements on all imported food.
Pork and alcohol are prohibited from import entirely, so a product legally on sale is unlikely to contain declared pork.
The stricter default profile reflects SFDA's position on doubtful additives.

MY.name: Malaysia
notes: MS 1500 is the national halal standard; the JAKIM logo is the authoritative mark.
JAKIM does not accept cochineal/carmine (E120) or wine vinegar.
Products bearing a valid JAKIM mark can be treated as halal without ingredient-level analysis.

ID.name: Indonesia
notes: Law 33/2014 makes halal certification mandatory for food circulating in Indonesia; BPJPH issues certificates on MUI fatwa.
Non-halal products must be explicitly labelled as such.
MUI treats carmine as impermissible.

GB.name: United Kingdom
notes: Retained EU labelling law: additives are declared by category plus name or E-number.
The 14 regulated allergens must be emphasised, so fish-derived gelatine and egg lecithin are detectable via the allergen statement.
HMC applies a stricter standard than HFA, notably rejecting mechanically stunned poultry.

EU.name: European Union
notes: Regulation 1169/2011 requires additives by functional class plus name or E-number, and emphasis of the 14 allergens.
Because fish is a declarable allergen, gelatine with no fish allergen flag is very likely bovine or porcine.
'Natural flavouring' is permitted without source disclosure, so it stays doubtful.
Regulation 1169/2011 Annex VI requires the specific animal species to be named for added meat ingredients.

US.name: United States
notes: FDA labelling uses common ingredient names, not E-numbers; do not expect 'E471' on a US label.
21 CFR 101.22 lets 'natural flavors' include animal-derived material with no further disclosure, which makes the term less resolvable here than in the EU.
Carmine and cochineal extract must be declared by name (21 CFR 73.100), so an undeclared carmine is unlikely.
Cane sugar in the US may be bone-char refined; beet sugar is not.
'Spices' and 'flavors' may lawfully hide individual components.

CA.name: Canada
notes: Ingredient names rather than E-numbers are used.
'Halal' claims are regulated: the certifying body's name must appear next to the claim (SFCR).

AU.name: Australia / New Zealand
notes: FSANZ uses bare INS numbers without the 'E' prefix, so '471' on the label means the same as E471.
Additive class names ('emulsifier (471)') are standard.

IN.name: India
notes: FSSAI mandates a green dot for vegetarian products and a brown/red dot for non-vegetarian ones.
A green veg mark rules out meat, fish and egg ingredients, which resolves most animal-source doubt on additives such as E471, glycerol and gelatine.
It does not resolve alcohol-carrier doubt.

PK.name: Pakistan
notes: PS 3733 is the national halal standard, administered by PSQCA.

TR.name: Türkiye
notes: The Halal Accreditation Agency (HAK) is the national accreditation authority; OIC/SMIIC 1 is the reference standard.
Labels use Turkish additive names alongside E-numbers.

SG.name: Singapore
notes: MUIS is the sole authority for halal certification; its mark is legally protected.

ZA.name: South Africa
notes: Multiple recognised certifiers; SANHA and MJC marks are the most widely seen.

profiles.strict: Resolves any scholarly disagreement toward caution. Insect derivatives, transformed alcohol products and bone-char processing are all avoided.
profiles.mainstream: The position common to most major certifiers: source-ambiguous additives are doubtful rather than prohibited, transformation (istihalah) is generally accepted for vinegar, and processing aids that leave no residue are permitted.
profiles.lenient: Accepts istihalah broadly, permits trace alcohol carriers below carry-over limits, and follows the Maliki position permitting insect derivatives.
profiles.JAKIM: Malaysian national standard MS 1500. Rejects carmine and wine vinegar.
profiles.MUI: Indonesian standard under BPJPH. Rejects carmine.
profiles.HFA: Halal Food Authority (UK). Accepts machine-stunned poultry; conservative on additives.
profiles.HMC: Halal Monitoring Committee (UK). Stricter; rejects mechanical stunning.
profiles.IFANCA: Islamic Food and Nutrition Council of America.
profiles.SFDA: Saudi Food and Drug Authority, applying GSO halal requirements.

vegan.label: Certified vegan / plant-based claim
vegan.note: A vegan claim excludes all animal and insect derivatives, which settles source-ambiguity for additives such as E471, glycerol and gelatine. It does not address alcohol carriers.

vegetarian.label: Certified vegetarian / India green veg mark
vegetarian.note: Excludes meat, fish and their derivatives. Dairy and egg remain, which are halal in themselves. Does not resolve insect-derived colours such as carmine, nor alcohol carriers.

halal_certified.label: Recognised halal certification mark on pack
halal_certified.note: A valid mark from a recognised body means the certifier has already audited the sources. Verify the mark is genuine and current.

kosher.label: Kosher certification mark
kosher.note: Kosher certification excludes pork and requires supervised sources, which removes most porcine doubt. It is NOT equivalent to halal: it permits wine and alcohol, and kosher slaughter is accepted by some halal authorities but not all.

plant_based_stated.label: Label states vegetable/plant origin for additives
plant_based_stated.note: e.g. 'emulsifier (mono- and diglycerides of vegetable origin)'.
